story: On August 15, 1977, Ohio State University's Big Ear radio telescope was scanning the cosmos for extraterrestrial intelligence. Days later, volunteer astronomer Jerry Ehman reviewed the computer printouts and spotted an astonishing alphanumeric sequence: 6EQUJ5. Stunned by the extreme intensity, Ehman circled the characters in red pen and scribbled 'Wow!' in the margin. Big Ear was fixed in position and relied entirely on Earth's rotation to sweep across the sky, meaning any fixed deep-space point source could only remain in its beam for precisely 72 seconds. The mystery signal rose and fell across that exact 72-second window, matching the mathematical profile of an extraterrestrial transmission. It blared near 1420 megahertz—the natural emission frequency of hydrogen, long predicted as the universal interstellar hailing channel. At its peak, it was 30 times louder than background space noise, yet repeated searches never detected it again.
angle: The mystery signal lasted exactly 72 seconds—the precise window Earth's rotation allowed the telescope to observe a single point in deep space before sweeping away.
disputed: Duration of the signal: S7 reports the signal lasted '2 to 2 1/2 minutes', whereas S1, S3, S4, S5, and S6 specify 72 seconds (matching Big Ear's beam transit time). The script should state 72 seconds.

The comet hypothesis: S2 and S6 present the comets 266P/Christensen and Gibbs as strong candidates, but S1 and S3 note astronomers dismissed or ruled out this hypothesis due to timing and radio emission levels. The script should attribute this as an unverified and contested proposal.

Exact frequency: S1 notes John Kraus reported 1420.3556 MHz while Jerry Ehman reported 1420.4556 MHz due to an oscillator purchasing typo, and S2 cites 1420.40575 MHz. The script should refer to it simply as 'around 1420 megahertz'.
